question: Before anyone presses an oil, what do people cook, burn and anoint with — and where do the first oil crops come from?
summary: For most of this folio fat is *animal* fat. The oldest way to get it is rendering, heating tissue until the fat separates ([[te1]]); the first dairy fat, butter, arrives with Neolithic herders milking sheep and goats ([[ec1]]); and by about 1600 BC the oldest known recipes, the Babylonian cooking tablets, start almost every dish with water and then fat ([[e1]]). In hot Mesopotamia butter is always clarified so that it keeps, the ancestor of ghee ([[ec6]]). Which fat a region uses depends on its climate and pasture before it depends on anything else ([[w1]]). Beeswax, a lipid but not a fat, turns up in Turkish pots from about 7000 BC ([[ec16]]). The Egyptian records call butter fat what a translator rendered ‘butter’, and name ox fat, goose fat and a cheese in a First Dynasty jar ([[ec19]]); China’s pigs and dogs give meat and fat from Yangshao to Shang, with no milk ([[ec22]]); and Harappan pots held mostly animal fat, with little sign of dairy ([[ec17]]).

The oil crops appear in the same long span, and their record is mostly botanical. The olive is domesticated in the Chalcolithic Levant ([[ec2]]), flax serves for oil and fibre ([[ec3]]), sesame is grown at Harappa and carried to Mesopotamia and Egypt ([[ec4]], [[x1]], [[x2]]), and by the Late Bronze Age Crete, Cyprus and the palace economies of the Levant press and store olive oil on a large scale ([[te2]], [[ec8]], [[ec9]]). Europe has its own northern oil seeds: the opium poppy, domesticated in the west Mediterranean, is found from La Marmotta in Italy to the Alpine lake villages; Camelina, a weed of flax, becomes central Europe’s oil crop; and wild crucifers are collected for oil in Swiss lake villages, as crushed brassica cakes already lie at Jerf el Ahmar ([[ec26]], [[ec25]], [[ec27]]). Far away, sunflower and soybean are domesticated on different continents with no contact between them ([[ec13]], [[ec14]]). Africa and the Americas enter at the margins: herders in the green Sahara heat milk in pots in the fifth millennium BC ([[ec10]]); oil-palm shells turn up at African sites from about 3000 BC on one unverified abstract ([[ec11]]); and peanuts are grown in Peru by 2000 BC ([[ec12]]). Kiple’s editors add why Africa south of the Sahara and the Americas lean on tree fats: the tsetse fly discouraged herds in one, and the other had few domesticated animals ([[th6]]). Egypt’s own best oil, nhh, is a name nobody can identify ([[th2]]). The north’s fat includes the sea: Baltic hunter-gatherers burn blubber lamps and keep cooking marine and freshwater food in their pots when farming arrives ([[te4]], [[ec15]]). The older story — bone grease, fat lamps and the first pots — is the folio before this one. Egypt’s own oils were ben, balanos, castor and lettuce, and its olive a rarity in the records ([[ec20]], [[ec21]]); the palm fat at Abydos is now contested, since Lucas rejects it ([[ec7]]). In the Americas the avocado is managed for bigger, thicker-skinned fruit from about 5600 BC ([[ec23]]), and in New Guinea the coconut, Canarium almond and candlenut turn up at waterlogged sites ([[ec18]]).

The folio's point is that fats and oils start as separate stories — herders' fat in the north and east, plant oil in the Mediterranean and the Indus — and that the evidence for the second is much firmer than for the first. Everything later in the program is the movement and substitution of these fats.

themes.title: The fat of animals and milk
text: Rendered tallow and sheep's tail fat, then butter and clarified butter: the herder's fats, and the ones the Babylonian cooks use. The evidence is textual and popular-historical, since the residue studies are not in the library.

themes.title: The olive, from tree to press
text: Charred stones show the tree under cultivation by about 4800–3800 BC; the first evidence of large-scale processing is Late Bronze Age Crete and Cyprus, with palace oil stores reported at Ebla, Mari and Ugarit. Stones and wood date the tree, not the oil.

themes.title: Sesame, the oil crop that travels
text: Sesame is grown at Harappa by about 2600 BC, reaches Mesopotamia by about 2000 BC with its names, is named as an 'oil-plant' in cuneiform from about 2400 BC, and is among Tutankhamun's grave goods. Its identification in the cuneiform is still argued.

themes.title: Other oils, and a doubtful soap
text: Flax for oil and fibre, mustard and linseed in the Indus, palm fat in an Egyptian tomb, and the independent domestication of sunflower and soybean; and a popular claim that soap was made in Babylonia by about 2500 BC, which no source in the library supports.

themes.title: Africa and the Americas: the fats the Mediterranean story leaves out
text: Dairy fat in Saharan pots, the African oil palm, and the New World’s peanut and sunflower. The African entries rest on thin tiers (an abstract, a 1897 analysis), but they show that the oil palm and herders’ milk fat are older than any written record of them. Kiple’s editors explain the pattern: few herds south of the Sahara and in the Americas left a gap that avocado, palm and coconut filled.

themes.title: Marine fats of the north
text: Blubber lamps and marine food in Baltic pots show sea fat in use beside the farmers’ animal fat; the blubber-lamp entry rests on a title alone.

themes.title: The question of milk
text: Sherratt’s hypothesis that milking came late, Fuller’s caution that cattle are not always milked, and Suryanarayan’s Indus pots, which show little dairy: three readings of when herds began to give fat.

themes.title: Egypt’s fats, and a correction
text: Butter fat, ox fat, ben and balanos oils, castor and the rare olive: what the Egyptologist can say, and why the Abydos palm-oil claim is not safe.

themes.title: Tree fats of the tropics
text: Avocado in Honduras, coconut, Canarium and candlenut in New Guinea, and oil-palm shells in Africa: tropical tree fats that were tended long before they were pressed.

themes.title: Europe’s northern oil seeds
text: Poppy, Camelina and the wild crucifers: plant oils of the cool north, found as seeds in Neolithic and Bronze Age sites, with the pressing itself unseen.

turning_points.text: Neolithic herders make the first butter.
The olive is domesticated in the Chalcolithic Levant.
Saharan herders process milk fat in pots.
Sesame is a crop of the Harappan Indus.
Sesame travels to Mesopotamia, with its name.
The Yale culinary tablets put fat in every pot.
Cyprus and Crete press olives at scale.

how_to_read: Start with *Economy* and *Exchange*, where the crops are, then *Technology* for the presses and for rendering. The fat groups run through the folio (Olive Oil, Oilseeds, Butter & Ghee, Palm & Coconut), so a reader can follow one substance across periods.
Most lanes are empty by design: there is almost no evidence for law, belief or conflict about fats before 1200 BC. The next folio is where the olive and sesame get states, gods and laws.

The *picture by region* counts the 43 entries: Europe 6, Near East 19, Far East 9, Africa 2, Americas 3, Oceania 1, Worldwide 3. Egypt, China, India, the Americas and Oceania each now have entries drawn from books or papers read, though the Near East still carries most and Africa has only two.

sources.intro: Prehistory is a story of plants and pots, so the folio leans on botanical syntheses, specialist volumes on sesame, and a translation of the Babylonian cooking tablets, with popular histories filling the gaps on butter and olive oil.
main: Zohary, Hopf & Weiss, *Domestication of Plants in the Old World*, for the olive and flax ([[ec2]], [[ec3]]).
Bedigian (ed.), *Sesame: The Genus Sesamum*, with Kiple's chapter and Achaya, for sesame ([[ec4]], [[x1]], [[x2]], [[th1]]).
Bottéro, *The Oldest Cuisine in the World*, for the Babylonian recipes and butter ([[e1]], [[ec6]]).
Foxhall, Kiple, Mueller and Khosrova for the olive's Bronze Age and for butter ([[te2]], [[ec8]], [[ec1]]).
Dunne et al. (through a search abstract) and Kiple for Saharan dairying and the peanut ([[ec10]], [[ec12]]); Lynn and one unverified abstract for the African oil palm ([[ec11]]).
Roffet-Salque et al., as abstracted, for Neolithic beeswax ([[ec16]]).

Lucas for Egypt’s fats and oils, read from a scanned copy by OCR ([[ec19]], [[ec20]], [[ec21]], [[ec7]]); Chang and Anderson for China ([[ec22]], [[th5]]); Suryanarayan 2021 and Fuller 2006 for the Indus ([[ec17]], [[th3]]); Sherratt 1983 for milking ([[th4]]); Kirch for Near Oceania ([[ec18]]); VanDerwarker 2025 for the avocado ([[ec23]]).
Bray (SCC 6.2) and Chang for the Banpo brassica seeds and the doubted early peanut ([[ec24]], [[th5]]).
Kiple’s editors for the missing herds of the tsetse belt and the Americas ([[th6]]).
Zohary, Hopf & Weiss for poppy, Camelina and the cruciferous oil seeds ([[ec26]], [[ec25]], [[ec27]]).
contested: The Akkadian 'oil-plant' as sesame rather than flax ([[th1]]); older statements that no sesame came from Mesopotamia are corrected by later finds ([[x1]]).
Palm fat at Abydos rests on one analysis of 1897 ([[ec7]]).
Palace oil stores at Ebla, Mari and Ugarit come from a journalist's summary ([[ec9]]).
The soybean's Chinese dating ([[ec14]]) and the Babylonian soap claim ([[te3]]) are unsettled.
Saharan dairy fat rests on an abstract and press coverage, not the paper ([[ec10]]); the oil-palm shells on one abstract ([[ec11]]); the identity of nhh is argued ([[th2]]).
The blubber lamps are known here only by an article title and context ([[te4]]); the Baltic lipid study only by its abstract ([[ec15]]).
Beeswax shows use of the honeybee, not beekeeping, and is a wax rather than a fat ([[ec16]]).

The Abydos palm fat is rejected by Lucas ([[ec7]]); the Chekiang sesame and peanuts are doubted by Chang and Anderson ([[th5]]); the Indus lipid result is hard to read without local reference fats ([[ec17]]).
‘An absence of animal fats’ is the editors’ general phrase and the folio’s own Saharan and hunter entries are exceptions ([[th6]]).

The Camelina dating in Zohary is internally inconsistent, ‘ca. 4,000 BC’ against the fifth and fourth millennia BP ([[ec25]]); the poppy, Camelina and brassica entries show seeds, not pressed oil ([[ec26]], [[ec25]], [[ec27]]).
gaps: Chinese oils before 1200 BC appear only as pig fat, a doubted find and a conjecture about brassica seeds ([[ec22]], [[th5]], [[ec24]]); Bray’s account of the oil crops is read for this, but not Wagner or the Chinese archaeological reports. Bray notes that the Chinese oil press is not described before the Sung.

Marine fats beyond the Baltic and Japan — the Arctic, the Pacific coasts, the Indian Ocean fish-eaters, Moseley’s Andean coast — are not covered; African fats other than the palm and Saharan milk (shea, Ethiopian oilseeds) are missing.
The Egyptian entries rest on Lucas, who wrote in the 1920s–60s; later work on Egyptian oils (Serpico & White) is not held.

text: Europe enters through the island palaces of Crete and Cyprus, where oil is pressed at scale ([[ec8]], [[te2]]), and through the northern oil seeds read from Zohary’s archaeobotany: the poppy from La Marmotta to the lake villages, and Camelina from Auvernier to the Baltic ([[ec26]], [[ec25]]). The north’s animal-fat world is described in the climate baseline ([[w1]]), and the sea fat of the Baltic is here too: marine and freshwater food in pots and the blubber lamps of the Late Mesolithic ([[ec15]], [[te4]]). Nothing in the library dates a European animal-fat practice before 1200 BC.

The core of the folio, because the evidence is here: the first butter and clarified butter, the Chalcolithic olive, flax, palace oil stores, the Babylonian recipes and the inspectors of Ebla ([[ec1]], [[ec2]], [[ec3]], [[ec9]], [[e1]], [[o1]]). Egypt is filed under the Near East in the atlas, though it is African: butter fat and the cheese at Saqqara, ben, balanos and castor oils, the rare olive, Tutankhamun’s sesame, nhh and the contested Abydos palm fat ([[ec19]], [[ec20]], [[ec21]], [[x2]], [[th2]], [[ec7]]), and Canaanite oil on the sea routes to Egypt ([[x4]]). Beeswax in Turkish pots from about 7000 BC is here as a lipid used later for candles and seals ([[ec16]]). Crushed brassica or mustard seed cakes at Jerf el Ahmar and carbonised seeds at Khafadje are the earliest hints of pressed or ground oil seeds ([[ec27]]).

The Harappan Indus: sesame, mustard and linseed, animal fat in the pots, and Fuller’s caution about assuming milk ([[ec4]], [[ec5]], [[ec17]], [[th3]]), with sesame’s journey west ([[x1]]). China has three entries: pigs and dogs for meat and fat with no milk, the doubted sesame and peanuts of Chekiang, and the soybean, whose domestication date (2700 or 1000 BC) is argued ([[ec22]], [[th5]], [[ec14]]). China’s earliest possible oil crop is also here: brassica seeds at Banpo, which may have been pressed ([[ec24]]).

Two entries, both at the thin end of the evidence: dairy fat in Saharan pots ([[ec10]]) and oil-palm shells at West and Central African sites ([[ec11]]). Egypt’s entries sit under the Near East, among them the correction of the Abydos palm claim ([[ec7]]). Nothing in the library covers shea, Ethiopian oilseeds or the Nile above Egypt in this period.

Three entries: the managed avocado at El Gigante, peanuts grown in Peru by 2000 BC with Kiple’s note that the New World had few fat animals, and the sunflower domesticated in eastern North America ([[ec23]], [[ec12]], [[ec13]]).
One entry: coconut, Canarium almond and candlenut at waterlogged New Guinea sites, 3800 to 2100 BC, from Kirch ([[ec18]]). They are fat-bearing nuts; nothing says oil was pressed.

The climate baseline that sets the fat by the land, Sherratt’s hypothesis on when people began to milk, and Kiple’s editors on why Africa south of the Sahara and the Americas, with few herds, lean on tree fats ([[w1]], [[th4]], [[th6]]).
